pos: n. (the Hanseatic city on the Gulf of Finland, now Tallinn; the chief Reformation town of Estonia)
etymology: From the Danish name of the district Revælæ; the Estonian Tallinn is from taani linn, the Danish town.
biblical_def: Reval was founded by the Danes, sold to the Teutonic Order, and grew into the Hanseatic port of the Gulf of Finland, a German-governed city with an Estonian-speaking majority outside the walls. The Reformation reached it in 1523 and 1524 through preachers in the town churches and was adopted by the council in 1525, making Reval the first Estonian town to go over. Images were destroyed in September 1524, and the city afterwards built its church order on the Lutheran model, with a Latin school, a poor chest, and preachers appointed to the Estonian congregation at the Holy Ghost church. That last provision mattered more than the rest: for a century and a half the Holy Ghost pulpit was where Estonian prose was first written down. The dictionary records the city as an instance of the gospel crossing a language line inside one town's walls, as it did first at Antioch: “spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus” (Act 11:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Hanseatic as pertaining to the Hanse towns and their commercial confederacy; a council as an assembly convened for consultation; and to publish as to make known to mankind, to proclaim.
webster_full: HANSEATIC, a. Pertaining to the Hanse towns, or to their confederacy for the protection of commerce.
COUNCIL, n. [L. concilium.] An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation or advice.
PUBLISH, v.t. [L. publico.] To make known to mankind or to people in general; to proclaim; to promulgate.
TIDINGS, n. News; advice; information; intelligence; account of what has taken place.
CONGREGATION, n. A collection or assembly of persons; an assembly met for the worship of God.
scriptures: And some of them were men of Cyprus and Cyrene, which, when they were come to Antioch, spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus.
Act 8:5
Then Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them.
Isa 52:7

How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
Act 16:9
And a vision appeared to Paul in the night; There stood a man of Macedonia, and prayed him, saying, Come over into Macedonia, and help us.
corruption_summary: The Hanseatic city on the Gulf of Finland, now Tallinn; the first Estonian town to adopt the Reformation, by council decision in 1525, with an Estonian pulpit at the Holy Ghost church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest reckoning is the same as Riga's. Reval's Reformation was made by German burghers for German churches; the Estonians of the lower town and the countryside were carters, servants and peasants with no voice in the council that voted it. The Holy Ghost appointment was a real concession and a small one. The dictionary records that the gospel reached the Estonians a generation late and through one pulpit, and that it did reach them.

The principle to recover is that the gospel crosses a language line as a matter of course, and that the first men to do it were not commissioned to. At Antioch unnamed Cypriots and Cyrenians simply started preaching to Greeks: “spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus” (Act 11:20). Philip does the same across the oldest enmity in Israel — “Then Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them” (Act 8:5). Isaiah's blessing is on the feet that carry it, not the throne that authorises it: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings” (Isa 52:7). And a call across water comes as a request for help (Act 16:9).

pos: n. (the Livonian bishop's city on the Emajogi, now Tartu; where the Reformation arrived with a fanatic attached to it)
etymology: From Estonian Tarbatu, germanised Dorpat; the modern Estonian Tartu preserves the older form.
biblical_def: Dorpat was the seat of a Livonian bishopric and a Hanseatic trading town on the Emajogi. Melchior Hoffman, a furrier with no training and great fluency, came there in 1524 and preached the Reformation with an apocalyptic edge; the town rose, the churches were stripped, and there was killing in the streets in January 1525. Bugenhagen and Luther both wrote to Dorpat urging order, and Luther's letter to the Livonians is one of his clearest statements that reform is not riot. Hoffman went on to Sweden and then to a career as a Melchiorite prophet in the Netherlands. Dorpat settled into a Lutheran town, and after Sweden took it the Academia Gustaviana was founded there in 1632, the north-east's first university. The dictionary records the city because the lesson it taught the Reformation was about the men it attracted: “Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fanatic as a person affected by excessive enthusiasm, particularly on religious subjects; perverse as obstinate in the wrong, untractable; and to wrest as to distort, to turn from the true meaning.
webster_full: FANATIC, n. [L. fanaticus.] A person affected by excessive enthusiasm, particularly on religious subjects; one who indulges wild and extravagant notions.
PERVERSE, a. [L. perversus.] Obstinate in the wrong; stubborn; untractable; disposed to cross and vex.
WREST, v.t. To twist or extort by violence; to distort; to turn from truth or from its natural meaning.
UNLEARNED, a. Ignorant; not instructed; not versed in a particular subject.
UNSTABLE, a. Not fixed; not firm; inconstant; irresolute; wavering.
scriptures: Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them.

As also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.
Tit 3:9
But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
Neither give heed to fables and endless genealogies, which minister questions, rather than godly edifying which is in faith: so do.
corruption_summary: The Livonian bishop's city on the Emajogi, now Tartu, where Melchior Hoffman's preaching in 1524 produced iconoclasm and killing; a Swedish university was founded there in 1632.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse of Dorpat is older and is made by both sides. Rome's controversialists used it, then and since, to prove that the appeal to Scripture ends in mobs; some Protestant accounts simply omit Hoffman. Neither will do. A man with no training, no call and immense conviction got a hearing in Dorpat precisely because the Reformation had taught people to listen to a preacher rather than an office, and that is the cost of a real good, not an argument against it. Luther's own letter to Livonia faced it squarely.

The principle to recover is that false teachers come out of the church's own membership and are to be expected, not merely lamented. Paul warns the Ephesian elders of exactly this source: “Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30). Peter names the mechanism — hard passages handled by unstable men who “wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction” (2Pe 3:16). The remedy is not more excitement but a refusal to be drawn into the ground they choose: “But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law” (Tit 3:9).

pos: n. (the Estonian town on the river of the same name, the frontier between the Lutheran west and the Orthodox east)
etymology: From the river name Narva, probably Finnic, from a root meaning a rapid or a waterfall.
biblical_def: Narva stands on the river that has been a boundary for seven centuries: the Order's castle on one bank, the Russian fortress of Ivangorod built facing it on the other in 1492, and the two staring at each other across two hundred yards of water. The town was Lutheran from the Reformation, taken by Ivan IV in 1558 at the opening of the Livonian War, held by Russia for twenty-three years as its one Baltic port, retaken by Sweden in 1581, and fought over again in 1700 and 1704. It is the plainest border in northern Europe, and the place where the Lutheran and Orthodox churches of the north have faced each other longest. The dictionary records it because Scripture treats national boundaries as appointed rather than accidental, and as limits rather than ends: “and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bound as a limit, the external or exterior line which incloses a place; a landmark as a mark to designate the boundary of land; and a frontier as the marches, the border of a country.
webster_full: BOUND, n. A limit; the line which comprehends the whole of any given object or space; the exterior line which incloses a place.
LANDMARK, n. A mark to designate the boundary of land; any mark or fixed object by which the limits of a farm are known.
FRONTIER, n. [L. frons, the forehead.] The marches; the border, confine, or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.
HABITATION, n. [L. habitatio.] Act of inhabiting; state of dwelling; place of abode; a dwelling.
REMOVE, v.t. To cause to change place; to put from its place; to displace.
scriptures: And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter.
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
Psa 97:1
The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof.
corruption_summary: The Estonian frontier town facing the Russian fortress of Ivangorod across the Narva river; Lutheran from the Reformation and fought over from 1558 to 1704.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live question Narva raises is whether a border is a thing a Christian may care about. Two answers are both wrong. The one treats a frontier as sacred, so that the nation on this side is God's and the nation on that side is not. The other treats every boundary as an arbitrary scar to be dissolved. Scripture does neither: it says boundaries are appointed by God for the dwelling of peoples, and in the same breath says the peoples on both sides are of one blood.

The principle to recover is in Paul's single sentence on the Areopagus, which puts unity and limit together and will not let either go: God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26). The Psalm credits the borders of the earth to the same hand that made the seasons — “Thou hast set all the borders of the earth” (Psa 74:17) — and Proverbs forbids the quiet theft of a neighbour's line (Pro 22:28). Over every such line one reign is announced: “The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice” (Psa 97:1).

pos: n. (the Estonian port on the Gulf of Riga, now Parnu; a Hanseatic harbour town and briefly a university seat)
etymology: From the river name Pernau, Estonian Parnu, from parn, the linden tree.
biblical_def: Pernau stands where its river meets the Gulf of Riga, and lived by the sea: a Hanseatic member exporting grain, flax and timber, with a harbour that made it worth taking in every war fought over Livonia. It went Lutheran with the rest of Estonia in the 1520s, passed from the Order to Poland, then Sweden, then Russia, and was burned and besieged repeatedly. In 1699 the Swedish university at Dorpat was moved to Pernau to get it away from the Russian frontier, and it taught there until the Great Northern War closed it in 1710. The town is otherwise unremarkable, which is the point: an ordinary trading harbour whose men got their living on water, and for whom the sailors' psalm was not a metaphor. “They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters” (Psa 107:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a haven as a harbour, a port, a place of safety for ships; business as employment, that which occupies the time and attention; and quiet as still, free from motion or disturbance.
webster_full: HAVEN, n. [Saxon haefene.] A harbour; a port; a bay or inlet of the sea where ships can ride in safety; a shelter, an asylum.
BUSINESS, n. Employment; that which occupies the time, attention and labour of men for profit or improvement.
QUIET, a. Still; free from motion or disturbance; peaceable; not turbulent.
HARBOUR, n. A lodging; a place of entertainment; a port or haven for ships.
COURTEOUSLY, adv. In a kind, civil, obliging manner; with complaisance.
scriptures: They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters;
Then are they glad because they be quiet; so he bringeth them unto their desired haven.
Act 27:3
And the next day we touched at Sidon. And Julius courteously entreated Paul, and gave him liberty to go unto his friends to refresh himself.
Isa 41:5
The isles saw it, and feared; the ends of the earth were afraid, drew near, and came.
corruption_summary: The Hanseatic port on the Gulf of Riga, now Parnu; Lutheran from the 1520s, and seat of the Swedish university from 1699 to 1710.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a habit worth resisting in how a town like Pernau gets written up: the search for significance, the hunt for the one famous man or decisive event that makes a place worth an entry. Pernau has very little of that. It had a harbour, a church, a school for eleven years, and a few thousand people who loaded grain and buried their dead. The dictionary includes it because God's providence is mostly spent on places like this one, and a dictionary that only records the summits has misrepresented the map.

The principle to recover is that ordinary labour at sea or anywhere else is where the works of the LORD are actually seen. The Psalm does not send the reader to a temple to find them; it sends him to a working crew: “They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters” (Psa 107:23). The end of that psalm's storm is not a vision but a harbour and a night's sleep — “so he bringeth them unto their desired haven” (Psa 107:30). Even in Acts a kindness at a quayside is written down (Act 27:3), and it is the coastlands that see and fear (Isa 41:5).

pos: n. (the Livonian Order's great castle in southern Estonia, now Viljandi; surrendered to the Russians by its own mercenaries in 1560)
etymology: From Estonian Viljandi, germanised Fellin; the Estonian name is probably from vili, grain or crop.
biblical_def: Fellin was one of the largest and strongest castles in Livonia, a frequent residence of the Order's Masters, with a town under its walls. In August 1560, in the second year of the Livonian War, the Russian army besieged it. The castle held the former Master Furstenberg, a full magazine, and a garrison of hired German troops whose wages were long unpaid. The mercenaries refused to fight, negotiated with the besiegers over their officers' heads, and handed over the strongest fortress in the country in exchange for free passage and money; those the Swedes caught afterwards were hanged. The castle was slighted and never recovered. The dictionary records Fellin because the Lord's own contrast between a shepherd and a hired man was acted out there in a single week: “The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep” (Joh 10:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hireling as one who is hired, or who serves for wages, and is used in contempt; mercenary as hired, that may be hired, greedy of gain; and to covenant as to bargain, to stipulate.
webster_full: HIRELING, n. One who is hired, or who serves for wages; it is often used in contempt, for a mercenary, a venal person.
MERCENARY, a. [L. mercenarius.] Hired; that may be hired; greedy of gain; influenced by the hope of reward.
COVENANT, v.i. [L. convenio.] To bargain; to stipulate; to enter into a formal agreement.
GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town for its defence.
WAGES, n. Hire; reward; that which is paid for service.
scriptures: But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep.
The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep.
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.
corruption_summary: The Livonian Order's largest castle, now Viljandi, handed to the Russian army in August 1560 by its own unpaid German mercenaries in exchange for passage and money.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The entry does require one piece of fairness. The mercenaries at Fellin had not been paid for a long time by a government that had run out of money, and men who fight for wages that stop coming have been wronged before they do wrong. That is a real mitigation and the dictionary states it. It is not an excuse. They did not mutiny and march away; they sold a fortress full of people to an army whose treatment of captured towns was known, and took payment for it.

The principle to recover is the Lord's own distinction, which is not between a brave man and a coward but between two kinds of relation to the flock. The hireling's flight is explained by what he is, not by his nerve: “The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep” (Joh 10:13); the shepherd stays because the sheep are his own (Joh 10:12). Paul traces the root of such a sale to one appetite — “For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10) — and the gospel records the actual bargaining, with a price named and agreed (Mat 26:15).

pos: n. (the largest Baltic island, now Saaremaa; a Livonian bishopric that became Danish and then Swedish Lutheran territory)
etymology: From Old Norse Eysysla, the island district; ey, island, and sysla, a district. The Estonian Saaremaa means island land.
biblical_def: Oesel is the great island off the Estonian coast, with the mainland district of Wiek, forming one of the four Livonian bishoprics. Its people were among the last and most stubborn resisters of the thirteenth-century conquest. Its last bishop, Johann von Munchhausen, sold his territories to Denmark in 1559 as the Livonian War began; Denmark held the island, made it Lutheran, and ceded it to Sweden in 1645. The island's Lutheran church kept Estonian in use earlier and more thoroughly than the mainland towns did, because there was no German burgher majority to preach to. The medieval bishop's castle at Arensburg still stands. The dictionary records Oesel because Isaiah's prophecies make a point of islands — the places on the edge of the map, named and addressed: “even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea” (Isa 24:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an isle as a tract of land surrounded by water, in Scripture often a maritime country; to glorify as to make glorious, to honour, to extol; and a multitude as a great number, a crowd.
webster_full: ISLE, n. [L. insula.] A tract of land surrounded by water; in Scripture, often a maritime country or coast.
GLORIFY, v.t. [L. gloria.] To make glorious; to exalt to glory; to honour; to extol; to praise.
MULTITUDE, n. [L. multitudo.] A great number of individuals; a crowd or throng; the populace.
ISLAND, n. A tract of land surrounded by water; a piece of land in a river or lake.
BISHOPRIC, n. A diocese; the district over which the jurisdiction of a bishop extends.
scriptures: Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the fires, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea.
Isa 51:5
My righteousness is near; my salvation is gone forth, and mine arms shall judge the people; the isles shall wait upon me, and on mine arm shall they trust.
Psa 97:1
The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof.
Isa 41:5
The isles saw it, and feared; the ends of the earth were afraid, drew near, and came.
corruption_summary: The largest Baltic island, now Saaremaa; a Livonian bishopric sold to Denmark in 1559, made Lutheran, and ceded to Sweden in 1645.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a condescension the entry exists to refuse. An island diocese in the Baltic is the kind of place church history mentions in a subordinate clause, and its inhabitants are treated as a residue to be governed rather than a people to be preached to. The record from Oesel is the opposite of that: because there were few Germans to preach to, Estonian preaching started earlier there than in Reval, and the island was better catechised than the mainland for a long stretch.

The principle to recover is that Scripture names islands deliberately and promises them a part. Isaiah does not say the nations in general but the furthest water: “Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the fires, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea” (Isa 24:15). Their part is not passive; they are given a posture of expectation — “the isles shall wait upon me, and on mine arm shall they trust” (Isa 51:5). The Psalm makes the reign over them the ground of their gladness (Psa 97:1), and the coastlands are the first to see and be afraid (Isa 41:5).

pos: n. (c. 1600–1657; superintendent in Estonia, author of the first Estonian grammar and handbook)
etymology: Stahl, a German surname from Stahl, steel; Heinrich, from Old High German heim, home, and rih, ruler.
biblical_def: Heinrich Stahl was born in Reval, studied at Rostock, Greifswald and Wittenberg, and served as pastor, then provost, and from 1641 superintendent of the Estonian church in Swedish Ingria and Estonia. Between 1632 and 1638 he brought out his Hand- und Hausbuch fur das Furstenthum Esthen in four parts: a catechism, the gospel and epistle readings, prayers and hymns, all in Estonian with the German facing, and a grammar of the language — the first ever written — so that German pastors could learn to preach in it. He also published a book of Estonian sermons. His Estonian is heavily Germanised and later writers criticised it hard; it was also the first usable tool any pastor had. The dictionary records him for the aim stated in his preface and in Nehemiah's Levites: to make the reading understood. “that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the LORD your God” (Deu 31:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; a handbook as a manual, a book for ready use; and to guide as to lead, to direct, to instruct and superintend.
webster_full: GRAMMAR, n. [Gr. gramma, a letter.] The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; a system of principles and rules for the use of a language.
MANUAL, n. [L. manualis.] A small book, such as may be carried in the hand, or conveniently handled; a handbook.
GUIDE, v.t. To lead or direct in a way; to conduct; to influence; to instruct and superintend.
ATTENDANCE, n. The act of waiting on; a giving heed to; close application.
SUPERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
scriptures: Gather the people together, men, and women, and children, and thy stranger that is within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the LORD your God, and observe to do all the words of this law:
Act 8:30
And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?
Act 8:31
And he said, How can I, except some man should guide me? And he desired Philip that he would come up and sit with him.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
corruption_summary: Superintendent of the Estonian church from 1641, whose Hand- und Hausbuch of 1632 to 1638 gave Estonian its first grammar, catechism and book of readings.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a scholarly judgment on Stahl that the dictionary should report and then weigh. His Estonian is bad: German word order, German idiom, a syntax no Estonian peasant would produce, and later writers from Forselius onwards had to undo much of it. That criticism is right. It is also true that before Stahl a German pastor sent to an Estonian parish had no grammar, no printed catechism and no readings, and after Stahl he had all three. A flawed instrument in hand beats a perfect one unwritten.

The principle to recover is that a hearer needs a guide and that providing one is a commanded ministry rather than a courtesy. Moses orders the whole population assembled, including the foreigner, for the purpose of comprehension: “that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the LORD your God” (Deu 31:12). The Ethiopian is reading the right book and asks the honest question — “How can I, except some man should guide me?” (Act 8:31) — after Philip has asked him the diagnostic one: “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Act 8:30). Timothy is told to give attendance to reading, exhortation and doctrine in that order (1Ti 4:13).

pos: n. (c. 1536–1600; pastor of the Holy Ghost church in Reval and chronicler of the Livonian war)
etymology: Russow, a Low German surname, probably from the place name Russow in Mecklenburg; Balthasar, from the Babylonian Belshazzar.
biblical_def: Balthasar Russow was born in Reval, probably of Estonian or mixed family, studied at Stettin and Wittenberg, and from 1562 until his death in 1600 was pastor of the Holy Ghost church, the Estonian-language congregation of the city. In 1578 he published his Chronica der Provintz Lyfflandt, a history of Livonia from the conquest to his own day, expanded in 1584 to cover the war he had lived through. It is the chief narrative source for the period, and what distinguishes it is that he wrote about the Estonian peasantry: their labour, their exactions, their famine, their abandonment by the lords who were supposed to defend them. The Livonian nobility attacked the book furiously and he answered them. The dictionary records him because an honest chronicle is a moral act, and Scripture ties speech to neighbourliness: “Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour” (Zec 8:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chronicle as a history or account of events in the order of time; truth as conformity to fact or reality; and a neighbour as one who lives near another, in Scripture any one whom we may benefit.
webster_full: CHRONICLE, n. [Gr. chronos, time.] An historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; a register.
TRUTH, n. Conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be.
NEIGHBOUR, n. One who lives near another; in a moral sense, one whom we may benefit, any fellow man.
LYING, n. The act of uttering falsehood; the habit of telling lies.
GENERATION, n. A single succession of men in natural descent; the people of the same period.

corruption_summary: Pastor of the Estonian-language Holy Ghost church in Reval from 1562, and author of the 1578 Chronica der Provintz Lyfflandt, the chief narrative of the Livonian war.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Russow raises a question about history-writing that is live in every generation: whether a man may write down what the powerful in his own country did to the powerless in it, while they are still alive and still powerful. He did, and they came for him, and the controversy over his chronicle ran for years. The dictionary notes that his own objectivity has limits — he is hard on the Order and the Catholic bishops and easier on the Swedes — and that he nevertheless recorded the Estonian peasants' sufferings when no one else was recording them at all.

The principle to recover is that truthful speech is owed to a neighbour as a debt, not offered as a favour: “Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour; execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates” (Zec 8:16). Paul grounds the same duty in membership: “Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another” (Eph 4:25). Proverbs sets the time-horizons side by side — “The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue is but for a moment” (Pro 12:19) — and a record kept now is kept for readers not yet born (Psa 102:18).

pos: n. (d. 1608; preacher at the Holy Ghost church in Reval, whose Estonian sermons are the oldest extended prose in the language)
etymology: Muller, a German surname from Muller, a miller; Georg, from Greek Georgios, a husbandman.
biblical_def: Georg Muller succeeded to the Estonian pulpit at the Holy Ghost church in Reval after Russow and preached there until his death in 1608. Thirty-nine of his Estonian sermons, delivered between 1600 and 1606, survive in manuscript and were published in 1891; they are by a long way the oldest extended prose in the Estonian language, and they were preached, not composed for a book. They were also preached in the worst years the city had known: plague, famine and the Polish-Swedish war, and the sermons name those things directly and call the congregation to repentance under them rather than to patience with them. His Estonian is more natural than Stahl's would be a generation later. The dictionary records him because preaching, and not literature, is what produced the language's first prose: “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a sermon as a discourse delivered in public for the purpose of religious instruction; preaching as the act of delivering a religious discourse; and engrafted as inserted into a stock, implanted.
webster_full: SERMON, n. [L. sermo, discourse.] A discourse delivered in public by a licensed clergyman for the purpose of religious instruction.
PREACHING, n. The act of delivering a religious discourse; a public religious discourse.
ENGRAFT, v.t. To insert a scion of one tree into another; to implant; to set or fix deep.
FOOLISHNESS, n. Folly; want of understanding; in Scripture, that which the world esteems folly.
MEEKNESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries.
scriptures: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.

Jas 1:21

And some of them were men of Cyprus and Cyrene, which, when they were come to Antioch, spake unto the Grecians, preaching the Lord Jesus.
corruption_summary: Preacher to the Estonian congregation at Reval's Holy Ghost church, whose thirty-nine sermons of 1600 to 1606 are the oldest extended Estonian prose.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a common inversion to refuse. The literary histories treat Muller's sermons as the beginning of Estonian prose, which they are, and so handle them as literature that happens to be religious. They are religious documents that happen to be literature: sermons on plague, famine and war, preached to people burying their children, calling them not to endurance but to repentance and to Christ. Reading them as specimens of early syntax is reading a doctor's notes for the handwriting.

The principle to recover is that faith is produced by hearing and that God chose preaching as the means on purpose. Paul states the order plainly: “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). He also concedes how unimpressive the means looks and insists the choice was deliberate — “it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe” (1Co 1:21). James tells the hearer how to receive it, with the thing taken in like a graft into living wood: “receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls” (Jas 1:21).

pos: n. (1683–1748; pastor at Juri and chief translator of the first complete Estonian Bible, 1739)
etymology: thor Helle, a Low German surname with the particle thor, at the, and Helle, a place name; Anton, from Latin Antonius.
biblical_def: Anton thor Helle was born in Reval, studied at Kiel, and from 1713 until his death in 1748 was pastor at Juri near Reval and an assessor of the Estonian consistory. He led the team that produced the first complete Bible in Estonian, printed at Reval in 1739 after about fifteen years of work in which the North Estonian dialect he used became the standard written language. He also wrote the grammar that accompanied it and a collection of proverbs and riddles gathered from his own parishioners. The 1739 Bible is the foundation of literate Estonian: a translation made for a peasant congregation, in their own speech, two hundred years after the Reformation had reached their towns. The dictionary records him for the result Scripture promises from exactly that act: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines entrance as the act of entering, the opening or beginning; the simple as the artless, the unlearned, those of plain understanding; and to accomplish as to complete, to fulfil, to perform.
webster_full: ENTRANCE, n. The act of entering into a place; the opening, passage or avenue by which a place may be entered; beginning, commencement.
SIMPLE, a. Artless; undesigning; sincere; unlearned; weak in intellect; not wise or sagacious.
ACCOMPLISH, v.t. [L. ad and compleo.] To complete; to finish entirely; to execute; to fulfil; to carry into effect.
VOID, a. Empty; vacant; having no effect; null; of no legal force.
UNDERSTANDING, n. The faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends the real state of things presented to it.
scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.

Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,

Gather the people together, men, and women, and children, and thy stranger that is within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the LORD your God, and observe to do all the words of this law:
corruption_summary: Pastor at Juri and chief translator of the first complete Estonian Bible, printed at Reval in 1739; his North Estonian became the standard written language.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The entry does have to record a cost honestly. thor Helle's Bible made North Estonian the standard, and in doing so it pushed the South Estonian of Tartu, which had received its own New Testament in 1686, to the margins; a dialect with its own Scriptures became a dialect without a future. That is a real loss, the ordinary price of a standard language, and the dictionary names it rather than celebrating 1739 as pure gain.

The principle to recover is that the Scriptures given to plain people do their own work, and that the work is light and understanding rather than mere literacy. The Psalm locates the effect at the threshold: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). God attaches a guarantee of effect to the word itself and not to the translator's skill — “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11). And even men with the text in their hands need the understanding opened to them by Christ: “Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Luk 24:45).
